back: The transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.
Transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant.
Transfer of pollen from an anther of a flower on one plant to a stigma of a flower on another plant of the same species.

front: Male parts of a flower and their functions
back: Stamen = anther (makes pollen) + filament (holds the anther up).

front: Female parts of a flower and their functions
back: Carpel = stigma (receives pollen) + style (holds the stigma up) + ovary (contains ovules; becomes the fruit).

front: Functions of sepals, petals and nectaries
back: Sepals protect the bud; petals attract insects with colour and scent; nectaries make nectar as a reward.
Small, dull or no petals; no scent or nectar; anthers dangling outside on long filaments; large feathery stigmas outside; huge amounts of small, light, smooth pollen.

front: Insect-carried pollen compared with wind-carried pollen
back: Insect: larger, sticky or spiky, fewer grains. Wind: small, light, smooth and dry, produced in enormous numbers.

front: Where are the male and female flowers of maize?
back: Male flowers in the tassel at the top; female flowers on the cob. Each silk is a long style leading to one ovule.

front: Self- vs cross-pollination: the key trade-off
back: Self: reliable but less variation, so less able to adapt. Cross: more variation and adaptability, but depends on pollinators or wind and wastes pollen.
Separate male and female flowers (maize, pumpkin); anthers and stigmas ripening at different times; separate male and female plants (pawpaw).
